newsitem.title: SPAIN: Copper prices seen boosted by deficits - Deutsche.
newsitem.headline: Copper prices seen boosted by deficits - Deutsche.

text.p: Copper prices are seen remaining high over the next 12 to 18 months, with the market likely to be in deficit both this year and in 1998, Wiktor Bielski, senior commodities analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said on Tuesday.

"The consensus view has been that the market has been about to move into surplus, but that view has been proved wrong over the last three years, when there have been deficits of between 100,000 and 250,000 tonnes," Bielski said at Metal Bulletin's International Copper Conference.
One of the factors had been that the market consistently under-estimated the strength of demand in the years 1994 to 1996.
Also, although there had been a 20 percent increase in mine production, the rise in smelting capacity had been less than nine percent -- hence smelter bottlenecks.
Meanwhile, copper's density of use, which had declined for 30 years, bottomed out three years ago and was now increasing.
"U.S. intensity of use has doubled, and where the U.S. leads the rest of the world follows," Bielski said.
Typically, U.S. copper use was on the rise in technological applications and vehicles, and these trends would spread to Europe and Asia.
The other principal factors were China and the current low level of stocks.
The Chinese Strategic Reserve Bureau (SRB) could import some 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes of copper to top up its stockpile, although this was an unknown element.

But with Chinese commercial stocks low, the country would need to import anyway, and given the scrap tightness the requirements would be for refined cathodes, somewhere between 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes a year for the foreseeable future.
There was also a seasonality to China's imports, with one third in the first half of the year and the balance in the second half.
"We would expect to see a much higher level of imports in the second half," he added.
Looking at stocks, these were currently at a low 3.2 weeks consumption, close to 1990's all-time low of 3.0 weeks, which was not presently being reflected in prices.
Demand would keep the market tight, and the stock ratio would drop to between 2.5 and 3.0 weeks.
"Although it is difficult to see prices getting to $1.60/lb, they could well get up to $1.50 on a spike basis if the fundamentals come through," he added.
